quotes.verbatim_quote:
The Harmonic Regions de1ine and organize the roles of each chord with regard to the key
    of a song, in addition to providing various replacement options for each of them. We have
    3 harmonic regions: ("C" major as reference)


    1- Root Region Chords (Tonic): Cmaj7 (I), Em7 (IIIm), Am7 (VIm).
    2- Subdominant Region Chords: (this group in divided into two groups):
    • Major: Fmaj7 (IV), Dm7 (IIm), Bbmaj7 (bVII).
    • Minor: Fm7(6) (7+) (IVm), Bb7 (bVII), Abmaj7 (bVI), Dbmaj7 (bII).

    3- Dominant Region Chords: G7 (V), Bø (VII).
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage is the foundational taxonomy of the entire chapter, naming all three harmonic regions and every chord that belongs to each, establishing the substitution logic that drives every subsequent section.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
• Root Region(Tonic):
     It gives the sense of resolution, rest or "being home" (key).

    • Subdominant Region:
     It gives the sense of movement and distancing, moving away from the tonic.

    • Dominant Region:
    It gives the sense of tension and instability, and wants to resolve to the tonic. With these three
    functions ( IV / V / I = distancing, tension and rest ), we generate what we call a cadence, which
    is a chord progression with a resolution effect that defines the music's path.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage defines the functional meaning of each harmonic region — tonic as rest, subdominant as distancing, dominant as tension — and introduces the term 'cadence' as the governing concept for all subsequent progression analysis.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
• Major 7th chords:
 Cmaj7, Cmaj7(9), C6 , C6(9), Cmaj7(#11), C6(#11) , C6(9)#11, Cmaj7(6), Cmaj7(6)9



• Minor 7th chords:
 Cm7, Cm7(9), Cm7(11), Cm7(9)11, Cm(maj7)9, Cm6, Cm6(9)



• Half Diminished chords:
 Dø, Dø(9), Dø(11), Dø(9)11, Dm7(b6)



• Dominant 7th chords leading to major chords (V degree):
 G7, G7(9), G7(b9), G7(#9), G7(13), G7(b13), G7(b9)b13, G7(#9)b13, G7(9)13,
 G7(b9)13, G7(#11), G7(b9)#11, Gsus9, Gsus13, Gsus(b9)
quotes.why_load_bearing: This catalogues the complete palette of available voicing tensions for each chord quality, giving the player an exhaustive reference for coloring any chord in a progression.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Dominant 7th chords that are not the Vth degree or a tritone substitution, are always
considered lydian dominant. In other words, we can use the following tensions on them:

• 9, 13, or #11. Even though this is a rule, remember that it can be broken, mainly when
we have modal harmonies.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is an explicit harmonic rule distinguishing how to tension non-functional dominant chords (lydian dominant: 9, 13, #11) from functional V-chord dominants, directly governing which extensions are safe to use.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
In theory, any chord of a given Harmonic Region may be replaced by another of the same region.
    Hence we will find the most famous cadence in popular music: IIm / V/ I. But notice that we
    had to replace the IVth degree by the IIm, which belongs to the same region.
    It is important to understand that a cadence does not have to be completed all the time.
    Sometimes we cannot play II / V/ I in the same bar, therefore we can simply play V/ I. Actually,
    a subdominant chord is used to delay the Dominant chord, giving more colors to the harmony.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is the core substitution rule of the method — same-region chords are interchangeable — and explains why the IIm can replace IV, which is the theoretical basis for every II/V/I substitution chart that follows.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
In minor keys we may use the Harmonic Regions as follows (“Cm” as reference):

1- Root Region Chords: Cm7 (I), Ebmaj7 (bIII)



2- Subdominant Region Chords: Fm7(6) (7+) (IVm), Bb7 (bVII), Abmaj7 (bVI),
                              Dbmaj7 (bII), Dø (II)


3- Dominant Region Chords: G7 (V), B˚ (VII)
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage extends the harmonic region framework to minor keys with its own chord membership list, establishing the parallel minor vocabulary the reader needs for all minor II/V/I exercises in the chapter.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
An important detail to notice in the cadence II/V/I in minor keys (IVm/V7/Im) is that the
dominant seventh chords almost always use altered tensions such as: b9, # 9, # 11, b13. The
major 13th can be used with some regularity in the chords, but it is still an exception. In the key
of Cm we can have the cadence: G7(b9)13 leading to Cm7 for example.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This rule specifies that minor-key V7 chords characteristically take altered tensions (b9, #9, #11, b13), distinguishing their treatment from major-key dominant chords and guiding harmonic choices throughout the minor cadence exercises.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Even though there are many possibilities, we can never forget that the most important thing
when comping is to follow the melody, which will “tell” us what the best chord options are.
However, when improvising we can be more free because we will create the melodies, so it
means that even if we have a pre-set harmony dictated by the music, we can use all the “colors”
we have learned before, playing single notes or even block chords.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage states a foundational performance rule distinguishing the constraint on comping (melody governs chord choice) from the greater freedom available when soloing, which frames how all the voicing options in the chapter should actually be applied.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
II degree = Dm7 is a dorian chord, which means that it could be Dm6 as well. Now comes the
tricky thing: the third inversion of Dm6 is Bø which is the II degree from the Am cadence. So
we conclude that both II degree are the same.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This analytical passage proves degree-by-degree that the major and minor II/V/I cadences share the same underlying chord structures, providing the theoretical justification for treating them as interchangeable in substitution contexts.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
As we know, dominant 7th chords resolve to their ‘I’ chord. However, in the diatonic chord
    series, we have only one dominant chord, (G7) and it resolves to the tonic chord (C). So,
    secondary dominants are dominant chords that resolve to the other harmonic >ield degrees.
    They don't belong to the harmonic >ield and have nothing to do with it, except for the chord
    that they were assigned to resolve to.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage defines the secondary dominant concept precisely — a non-diatonic dominant whose sole relationship to the key is the degree it resolves to — establishing the term and logic used throughout the secondary dominant exercises.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
It is important to understand that subdominant chords are a way to delay the dominant
chord, that is why subdominant chords and dominant chords are interchangeable.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This concise rule explains the functional equivalence of subdominant and dominant chords in the II/V/I framework, directly authorising the many substitution swaps demonstrated in the exercises that follow.

quotes.topic: Dominant chord alteration rule for degrees
quotes.verbatim_quote:
Notice that, for a matter of organization and didatic, we apply dominant chords with altered
notes only for minor degrees. But actually, we can use any alteration to any dominant chord
leading to major or minor. However, we must make sure the altered notes we choose can be
applied over the song we are playing, because the melody will always determine what we
can and can not use. On the other hand, when we are improvising, we are much more free to
add any chord substitution in order to create movement and tension to the solo.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage corrects the pedagogical simplification used in the exercises and states the real rule: melody governs which alterations are permissible over any dominant chord, while improvising permits freer substitution choices.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
We can replace a dominant 7th chord by another dominant 7th chord just by changing the
     bass of the chord with its tritone. I.e. if the chord is G7, the replacement will be Db7. The
     reason we can do this exchange is that both have the same tritone:
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage gives the precise definition and mechanical rule for tritone substitution — replace the root with its tritone interval — and provides the theoretical justification (shared tritone) for why the exchange works harmonically.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Notice that dominant 7th chords such as 7(b9), 7(#9), and 7(b13), can be considered as
being the same, therefore they have the same function. Another important thing to notice
is that depending on the dominant chord we apply the tritone substitution to, it may not
sound correct or great. Example:

• C7(9) using a tritone substitution would be Gb7(b13), which most of time does not work.
So we replace the Gb7(b13) by Gb7(#11). However, in a cadence leading to Fmaj7 such
|| Gm7 | C7(9) | Fmaj7 || we should also change the voicing from the 1st chord as well.
Therefore, we would have: || Gm7(11) | Gb7(#11) | Fmaj7 ||.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage adds a critical practical rule to tritone substitution: when the substituted chord sounds wrong, adjust both the tritone chord's tension and the preceding II chord's voicing, illustrated with a concrete before/after example.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
However, remember that on the guitar we must learn things considering the
     5th string as the root and also the 6th string as the root. Therefore, below we have examples
     in the keys of "Cm" (root on the 5th string) and "Gm" (root on the 6th string)
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage states a guitar-specific positional rule — every key must be learned from both the 5th-string root and the 6th-string root — which is why the exercise sets are always presented in two complementary keys throughout the chapter.
